item.title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear, well-structured explanation of a complex phenomenon with useful vocabulary.

Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t.

What is sound hypersensitivity?

For some people, everyday sounds become hard to bear. Some researchers call this sound hypersensitivity, an umbrella term for several conditions.

There’s some disagreement about the names and definitions of these conditions, which makes it hard to determine how common they are. One of them is noise sensitivity, a tendency to feel annoyed or overwhelmed by ongoing background noise. Others include hyperacusis, in which ordinary sounds feel uncomfortably loud or even painful; misophonia, or intense anger, disgust or anxiety in response to specific sounds (For example: another person’s breathing); and phonophobia, the fear that a sound will cause discomfort.

What causes sound hypersensitivity?

Scientists don’t fully understand why everyday sounds become hard to tolerate for certain people. Daniel Polley, a neuroscientist who directs the Lauer Tinnitus Research Center at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, suspects some of the discomfort is a natural response to an increasingly industrialized and noisy world full of sounds we can’t control.

“As we age, we get a bit more rigid about what it is that we want going into our bodies,” he says, “including sound waves”.

That said, researchers are investigating a range of possible explanations. They haven’t pinned down a brain change that explains any one type of sound hypersensitivity, but people at higher risk for certain types include those with hearing loss, tinnitus (chronic ringing or buzzing in the ears), and neuropsychiatric conditions like autism. Much of what’s known about possible mechanisms of sound hypersensitivity comes from rodent studies, so there are still big questions about what’s happening in people.

A leading theory is called central gain, which relates to hearing loss. According to this theory, when damage to the inner ear weakens the signal it sends to the brain, the brain turns up its own amplification to compensate. As a result, it perceives a small increase in volume as much larger, which makes sounds seem louder than they really are. “The perception of sound isn’t generated in the ear; it’s generated in the brain,” says Polley.

Possible triggers are changes to the inner ear caused by age, noise exposure, or both. These can result in the loss of cells that amplify sound, and fraying of the auditory nerve that carries those cells’ signals to the brain.

Some people with sound hypersensitivity have hearing loss they don’t know about. Routine testing may not clarify things either, because standard hearing tests don’t pick up auditory nerve damage. As a result, some people with this type of hearing loss may struggle to follow conversations in noisy places but pass a hearing test.

What can you do about sound hypersensitivity?

There’s no medication that reliably eliminates sound hypersensitivity or reverses inner ear damage. However, certain strategies can lower your risk and ease symptoms.

The most important preventive step is to protect your ears from loud noise. Long or repeated exposure to sounds at 85 decibels or more, like those from speaker-heavy concerts, lawnmowers and leaf blowers, can damage your hearing. Wearing ear protection can delay that damage, although some wear comes with age no matter what.

If you suspect you already have some sound hypersensitivity, noise-canceling earbuds can quickly cut loud background noise while still letting you hear sounds you choose, says Polley. Earplugs also work, but they block everything, including sounds you may need or want to hear.

Just be aware that overprotecting your hearing can backfire. Shutting out too much sound may prompt the brain to turn up its amplification even further, which can worsen sound hypersensitivity. In one small study, people with normal hearing who wore earplugs for two weeks became less tolerant of loud sounds. “Isolating yourself, like going monastic, is not necessarily the right approach,” says Polley.

In one trial, people who did cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) tolerated louder sounds. This type of talk therapy can help sufferers avoid sounds less, face uncomfortable sounds gradually and feel less threatened by them. Some kinds of sound hypersensitivity are closely tied to anxiety and depression, and it’s possible treating those conditions can reduce symptoms.

When should you see a clinician?

Get help if sound hypersensitivity is causing you a lot of anxiety, disrupting your sleep or getting in the way of daily life, says Polley. Audiologists are usually the first point of contact. They can test your hearing and refer you to other specialists if needed.

If sounds hurt your ears, you may require a more cautious treatment approach. See a clinician, who may order brain imaging to rule out a growth on the auditory nerve.

If you have tinnitus, mention it to your clinician, as it often comes with sound hypersensitivity. Also take note if only one ear is affected; this may point to a specific cause that needs attention.

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-22 17:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: An age gap isn’t always a problem, partner abuse is | Letters
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with a personal account that adds depth to the discussion.

Regarding Polly Hudson’s article (At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now, 15 November), I met and lived with a 35-year-old man when I was 17. It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference.

The men doing this are rarely satisfied, and criticism can escalate to coercive, emotionally abusive levels. In some cases (though not in mine) girls are pimped out, shared with the man’s friends, imprisoned against their will.

To girls impressed by confidence, older men initially seem a catch. As for the father-daughter dynamic, a psychologist needs to pick apart why a grown man wants a sexual partner whom he treats like a daughter. I was seeking the father’s unconditional love and guidance that I never had. We’ve all heard of “daddy issues” – why do some men have “daughter issues”?

Name and address supplied

Polly Hudson should not be angry with her younger self. Would she be angry with another young girl who found herself in similar circumstances? Unlikely. There is something else that has stopped us speaking out: fear. Fear of physical or verbal retaliation by the perpetrator; of the judgment of those around us; of a legal system that fails to punish abusers and shames victims with hackneyed tropes that have long been disproven; of public and private organisations that continue to bury abuse allegations and enable perpetrators who bring in cash, clicks, viewers or shareholders.

Nevertheless, the more we talk, the harder it is for them to get away with it. Things are painfully slowly changing.

Michelle Stiles

Falmouth, Cornwall

It may be wise to increase the age of consent to 18 and I believe that victims of abusive relationships or rape need much better support. But the implications that arise from Gaby Hinsliff’s article (Don’t wait for a change in sexual consent law. Adults can act to stop age-gap abuse, 17 November) made me extremely uncomfortable.

My first serious relationship was with a man aged 33 when I was 18. He was both loving and affectionate, but the way in which people were so judgmental of both of us, and the implication drawn by other people that he must have been a pervert, made the relationship impossible.

I am now in my 30s and will be marrying a man in his 50s next month. We know that some people judge us based purely on our ages. It has made me reluctant to even post photos online of us as a couple. The only time that I have been in a relationship with an abusive element, the man was just a year older than I was. But there was never any automatic negative assumption about my relationship with him by others.

I want all victims of abuse to be empowered to seek justice and be supported in doing so. But there is a serious danger that we will reinforce the worst negative stereotypes of age-gap relationships while at the same time creating a false belief that relationships between people of the same age, or just a few years difference, are somehow inherently less likely to involve abuse or manipulation.

Ste Richard

Bristol

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-22 16:52 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The link between nurturing and masculinity | Letter
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Thought-provoking letter that challenges societal norms with clear, well-argued points.

Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s research offers an important challenge to one of our most persistent assumptions about masculinity: that nurturing is somehow contrary to male nature (Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so, 17 November). As a clinical psychotherapist, I find the most compelling implication is not simply that children benefit from involved fathers, but that fathers themselves may change through the experience of caring.

We often imagine psychological development as a process in which attitudes must change before behaviour follows. Yet caregiving may work in both directions. Repeated experiences of responding to another person’s vulnerability can engage and potentially strengthen the biological and psychological systems involved in emotional responsiveness, attachment and cooperation.

But we should be cautious about extending this into the claim that more nurturing fathers would necessarily produce a more peaceful world. Human beings are capable of extraordinary tenderness towards their own children while remaining hostile towards those outside their immediate circle. Empathy can be selective, and the causes of collective violence extend far beyond individual temperament.

Perhaps the more important question is whether the emotional capacities developed through caregiving can be extended towards strangers, communities and people with whom we disagree.

The significance of Hrdy’s work is not that nurturing makes men less masculine. It is that nurturing was never incompatible with masculinity in the first place.

Gareth Strangemore-Jones

Founder, Mental Health Matrix

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-22 16:50 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Kindness of strangers: I was stuck sitting in a sea of legs and feet when a beautiful young man offered me his hand
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Heartwarming personal story that demonstrates the impact of small acts of kindness.

My knees aren’t in terribly good condition. I’m at that age.

A few years ago, I was at a big hippy festival out in the Australian desert near Deniliquin. There, I attended a talk and was sitting down on the ground at the rear of a large group of people listening to a speaker. When the talk finished, everybody got up to leave, streaming past me as they went.

My fragile knees make it difficult for me to get up off the ground, and I didn’t want to attempt the manoeuvre in a crowd of people churning around me. So I thought, well, I’ll just sit here until they’ve all walked past, and then I’ll get up.

It was a bit humiliating sitting there in a sea of legs and feet; dust kicking up around me. Embarrassed, I had my head down.

And then this hand just appeared in front of me. I understood the gesture, which was, “Do you want help getting up?” I took the hand and, as the person pulled me to my feet, I saw it was a beautiful young man in his 20s. Once I was on my feet, we just smiled at each other. He walked off to do whatever he was going to do next, and I did the same.

For a woman getting into the age bracket where young men, in particular, don’t see you – in fact, they often have the propensity to not just ignore you but actively be rude – it challenged all my notions of who to be wary of, and who I could count on. This young man took the time to notice the middle-aged woman sitting in the dust and didn’t just walk past. He reached out, with an offer of humanity so perfect and so genuine.

That stranger, decades my junior, taught me that it only takes a second to make someone feel seen, and that second can make all the difference to your day, or your experience of yourself. I hope he’s gone on to have a fabulous life.

item.title: ‘I wouldn’t say top 20 in the world, but it’s the best in Adelaide’: a day in Ebenezer Place, one of the world’s coolest streets
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging article about a unique location with cultural context and vivid descriptions.

There’s a now-iconic line from The Simpsons, which aired more than 30 years ago, where Principal Skinner is trying to track down Bart, who has skipped school.

He goes looking for him in places he assumes children might hang out, including a museum and a youth group, but finds them empty.

He pauses and considers: “Am I so out of touch? … No. It’s the children who are wrong.”

I find myself asking a similar question perched on Ebenezer Place in Adelaide, recently ranked the world’s 19th coolest street by Time Out magazine.

Sipping on a glass of Gamay at 4pm on a Saturday at French brasserie Hey Jupiter, I look down the street to assess the level of “coolness” that convinced a global magazine this is one of the 28 streets in the world most worth visiting.

Adelaide is no stranger to the dizzying highs of global magazine lists, placing in the top 10 of the Economist’s most liveable cities index for eight of the past 10 years, much to the bemusement of the higher-ranked Melbourne and Sydney. But this time it has won out: the only other Australian entry on the Time Out list – Ward Avenue in Sydney’s Potts Point – is ranked No 24.

In coolness, Adelaide wins.

Hey Jupiter is softening me to this idea. The French brasserie, with its vibrant green facade, sits alongside a South African eatery, vintage clothing outlet, record store and a jeweller.

The tree-lined street is open to one-way traffic and cars circle looking for a prime parking spot. Yet despite this it’s clean, bright and well-manicured, much like the crowd of young fashionistas and well-dressed older couples soaking up the vibe and sipping everything from vibrant matcha to lethal-looking martinis.

Almost two decades ago, that would have been me.

While diligently avoiding my university lectures, I would waste days – and nights – at a clothing store owned by my two best mates, which opened here in the mid-2000s.

I certainly thought it was cool then.

Edgy fashion outlets attracted musical acts like Van She and Pnau, who would randomly arrive along the strip with drinks in hand from a nearby wine store, as music wafted out of the shopfronts.

With street parties and events sponsored by big tobacco, there was a time when this street was the wild west of Adelaide’s east end.

Twenty years later, Ebenezer Place has had a glow-up, got some new roommates and been officially recognised as cool.

Christopher Arblaster, co-founder of clothing store Shop Pond (formerly A Flat Shop), also runs the adjacent vintage store, Filter Store. While surprised by the nomination, he’ll happily take the hype.

“I think it shows more about the people who use the street. We have lovely neighbours, some really great shops and there’s quite a lot of activity along here for a quieter strip,” he says.

“I wouldn’t say it’s the 19th coolest street in the world – but it is a nice place to be.”

Surprise shout-out

It’s not that Ebenezer Place doesn’t deserve the accolade – but what, exactly, are the criteria?

Time Out recommends visitors to the street “keep the vibes high” at nearby drinking haunts Nola and East End Cellars, catch an indie film at Palace Nova, or dine at Michelin Guide-recognised restaurants Golden Boy and Africola.

It names Ebenezer Place as the destination but suggests you widen the net some 500m to visit other restaurants on the city’s edge. It also points readers towards Rundle Street for its indie boutiques and high-end fashion labels.

The City of Adelaide seems equal parts excited and caught off-guard about the shout-out, posting a gushing message to social media with a photo of the wrong East End strip – bustling Vardon Avenue, not Ebenezer Place.

As 21-year-old Nicolas Garcia-Bellido Rodriguez and his mate, 20-year-old Eamon Ziersch-O’Connor, enjoy an ice-cream at Ovo Coffee and Gelato, they say the strip evokes another continent entirely.

“It feels like I’m in Europe sitting here, and parts of Rundle Street feel the same too,” Nicolas says.

“I think it’s the proximity – it’s right near the Exeter hotel, which is great. It hosts a lot of events here, which I think contributes to the vibe.”

Ata Alrimawi, 22, says the strip is his go-to place to relax and grab a coffee.

“I wouldn’t say top 20 in the world, but it’s the best in Adelaide for sure,” he says.

The state MP and minister for Adelaide, Lucy Hood, says the global ranking speaks to the passion and dedication of local businesses that have transformed Ebenezer Place into “a thriving and must-visit destination”.

A subjective list will always attract clicks and is rarely without its controversies. As my Gamay reaches the end of its final pour and the afternoon slips into evening, the people-watching has provided hours of entertainment.

I would still argue the judges must have had a pretty biblical night along this street to convince them it’s one of the 20 best in the world.

But Ebenezer Place has always had its charms. As the sun fades, I decide to embrace this new, if surprising chapter in the story of this understated 120-metre long strip. Maybe it’s me who’s out of touch, and the children were right all along.

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-22 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/23/a-day-in-ebenezer-place-adelaide-one-of-the-worlds-coolest-streets

item.title: Readers reply: when does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Reader engagement piece with varied opinions, but lacks depth in analysis.

I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email

Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com.

Readers reply

When does a reasonable train route become unreasonable? When it’s no longer on track. Sagarmatha1953

I’ll guess that an Edinburgh to London route that involves a two-week stopover in Paris will not be considered “reasonable”. DeclineToState

Surely just any route in a roughly straight line to where you are going? The only catch would be when you’ve bought a split ticket using specific companies. My daughter recently had a cancelled train travelling from Glasgow to Leeds, but because it was a split ticket via Carlisle, anything on the east coast line was out of the question. On the plus side, she’d paid a small amount extra for some insurance and got £50 back for a £20 ticket (student railcard, before anyone gets excited by the price). She also found that, contrary to my expectations, the staff in the information desk at Glasgow station were incredibly helpful, so that’s probably a good place to start. Esollec

Since flying tends to be cheaper than trains, on this journey it would in theory be reasonable, but I doubt they’d consider it so. Plus the cost to the environment may not be thought reasonable. LorLala

The public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? I suspect when it comes to making a claim for a delayed or cancelled journey, it means you have a battle on your hands. salamandertome

It would be reasonable to go from Edinburgh to London via Glasgow. It would be unreasonable to go via Glasgow and Plymouth. thenewschmoo

Of course. But there are more nuanced journeys, aren’t there. These are extremes. But there is a line that will differentiate reasonable and unreasonable, and I guess the letter-writer wants to know how that is determined and by whom. lexicon_mistress

There’s a set of routing guides that covers most situations: for instance, if you want to go between London and Edinburgh you can go via Glasgow, via Sheffield, via Leeds, via Doncaster, etc. This is always allowed if you have an Any Permitted Route ticket. If you have a ticket which specifies an operator or a route, then it may be acceptable to take a different route. You’d need to check with staff. TheNewNo2

I don’t want to research train routes myself – I want an employee of the railway company to be on hand to advise me. This is why I always go by car, although Edinburgh to London is a bit of a stretch. Goldgreen

An actual person on hand to give actual advice? What a quaint concept these days … Kevcoe

There are rules, obviously. A direct train is always reasonable, however circuitous the route. As is a route up to three miles longer than the shortest possible route. Passing through the same station twice isn’t generally reasonable, apart from a specific list of “easements” where it makes sense to take a fast train that passes through your final destination shortly before stopping at major hub or terminus. You might think that any route that is faster than the shortest route is also reasonable, but this isn’t automatic. Strictly speaking, you need to check the manual, as other answers have said. During significant disruption (when it is announced that other companies are accepting tickets), staff apply their discretion, which was a bit of a lottery. Until last month, when we got the right to travel by any route suggested by the National Rail journey planner. MickeyFinn

An extra three miles doesn’t give options anywhere except major cities! zxcv11

It reads more like a chance or community chest card joke, so I’m not sure they are being serious. Luxembourgpro

Absolutely true, although I agree it sounds like parody. It’s called the Common Routing Point Rule. The National Routing Guide glossary (quoted below) is very clear on this point. MickeyFinn

When a journey is between stations that have one or more common routeing points, the permitted journey takes the route of shortest distance or any route no more than 3 miles longer, whether or not they pass through the common routeing point. Also permitted are journeys that use direct trains to and from the common routeing point.

A reasonable train route becomes unreasonable when the fare is too high. I always check for split-ticketing options and go the long way round if it’s cheaper, and not too much further. Much more reasonable! Rattandy

I reckon you’d have a reasonable case as long as you’re heading in the right general direction. Grumpyoldgit999

I’d say the quickest alternative route by train, assuming at least five minutes leeway each time you change trains, is the reasonable route. Anything other than that and they could argue that your ticket isn’t valid. That’s if they check the ticket – which they often don’t, particularly when staff are having to deal with disruption. RobertMeyerFunnell

The question-setter almost certainly has a ticket issued by a specific train company – LNER for the east coast mainline or Avanti for the west coast line. Normally, you have to travel on the line that you bought a ticket for, but if that’s disrupted you can use the other one. If everyone went on the faster east coast route then it would be overloaded, so it’s reasonable to spread the passengers across both east and west coast lines. It would be unreasonable if Edinburgh passengers tried to cut back to the east using the Settle or Transpennine lines, as then I would never get a seat. Randomusername222

If the people making that announcement can’t tell you, how are you supposed to know?…

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-22 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 50/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2026/nov/22/readers-reply-when-does-a-reasonable-train-route-become-unreasonable

It’s always a thrill to get new things – your favorite sweater in every color, the newest phone to hit the market – but you will get a lot more joy from a product that lasts years, decades or maybe even a lifetime.

At the Filter US, our mission is to help you buy fewer, better things. That mission is put to the test when Black Friday rolls around. There are a lot of enticing deals out there, but not every product on sale has enduring, lasting usefulness.

To help you sort through the noise, we have put together a collection of Black Friday deals that have proven themselves in our hands-on product testing, from a cast iron pan that will outlive us all to a travel-expert-approved backpack with a lifetime warranty.

We test products here at the Filter US and handpicked these deals. You can learn more about us at the bottom of the list. Products marked (sold out) are out of stock or no longer discounted. We’ll update our guides throughout Black Friday.
